zone: Goat Rocks and Mount St. Helens
_areas_note: Two unrelated access systems held in one file because the peaks were grouped that way. Goat Rocks: Berry Patch and the Snowgrass Trail trailhead off Forest Road 21 south of Packwood serve Old Snowy, Ives Peak and Gilbert Peak's western side; Conrad Meadows at the end of the South Fork Tieton road on the dry east side serves Gilbert Peak's Conrad and Meade Glacier routes. Gilbert was checked specifically and is NOT misassigned — it is genuinely a two-trailhead peak, but the split matters: the two glacier routes are Conrad Meadows objectives roughly 12 miles in from the east, while the West Route is the long southwest-slope scramble out of Snowgrass Flat via Cispus Basin. A party planning the Conrad Glacier from Berry Patch has picked the wrong side of the range. Mount St. Helens: Climbers Bivouac for Monitor Ridge in summer, Marble Mountain Sno-Park for Worm Flows the rest of the year. Pinto Rock, a small multi-face volcanic crag in the Cispus drainage, was deliberately left out — it is a roadside rock-climbing area, not an alpine objective, and needs nothing from this file.

sites.name: Snowgrass Flat area backcountry camps
sites.capacity: Numerous established sites in the timber and benches below and around the meadow; no quota and no numbered pads, so capacity is whatever the pre-existing sites hold, and on summer weekends that is fully subscribed
sites.water: Goat Creek and its tributaries run through the basin and are reliable well into the season; treat everything
sites.permit: Goat Rocks Wilderness permit, free and self-issued from the box at the trailhead — no reservation and no fee. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at Berry Patch or the Snowgrass trailhead. CAMPING WITHIN SNOWGRASS FLAT ITSELF IS PROHIBITED, along with camping within 100 feet of the Pacific Crest Trail and within 100 feet of any lake. Camp only in pre-existing sites.
sites.notes: The standard base for Old Snowy and Ives Peak, and for the West Route on Gilbert. The name misleads: the flat proper is a closed meadow and the legal camping is in the timber and on the benches a little below it, around 6,000 to 6,300 feet, roughly three to four miles from the road. From here Old Snowy is a walk-up on a spur off the crest, Ives is a scree-and-ridge scramble off the col between the two, and Gilbert is a long committing day traversing goat ledges across Cispus Basin at 7,400 to 7,600 feet before the southwest slope. This is the most heavily used corner of the wilderness and the parking fills on weekdays, so arriving Friday evening for a Saturday climb is a poor plan. The meadows hold snow into July in a normal year, which is pleasant for the scrambles and awkward for finding a dry pitch.

sites.name: Goat Lake basin
sites.capacity: A modest number of established sites scattered back from the shore; the closest ground to the water is off limits, which cuts the usable count sharply
sites.water: The lake, plus outlet streams; the lake can stay partly frozen into midsummer, in which case take water from the outlet
sites.permit: Same free self-issued wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass as the rest of this trailhead. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED within a quarter mile of the lake shore, so bring a stove and do not plan on a fire. The 100-foot setback from lakes applies here and is actively enforced by the condition of the ground.
sites.notes: The other basin camp on this side, reached by the loop that swings north from the Snowgrass trail, and a reasonable alternative when the Snowgrass sites are taken. It sits under Old Snowy's western flank and is slightly further from the crest than Snowgrass, which costs you distance on a summit morning but buys a quieter night. The basin is a cirque and holds snow late, so early-season parties frequently find the lake iced and the campsites buried — the trade for a genuinely alpine setting. Vegetation here is fragile and slow-growing, which is why the existing sites are the only acceptable ones.

sites.name: Dana Yelverton Shelter site
sites.capacity: A handful of small tents on the crest at best; there is no shelter left to sleep in and the ground is broken rock
sites.water: None. Snow patches persist nearby into midsummer and can be melted, but from late summer this is a dry camp and water must be carried up from the basin
sites.permit: Free self-issued Goat Rocks Wilderness permit. CAMPFIRES ARE SPECIFICALLY PROHIBITED at this location by wilderness regulation, and the 100-foot setback from the Pacific Crest Trail applies — the trail passes right through, so a legal pitch here takes some walking.
sites.notes: A named point on the crest just below Old Snowy, where a stone shelter once stood and where a hiker died in a summer blizzard in the early 1960s. The shelter is now a scatter of rubble and offers no protection whatsoever, so treat the name as a map label rather than a resource. Its value is position: it is the highest place on this side you can legally sleep, which shortens a summit morning on Old Snowy to almost nothing and puts Ives within an easy pre-dawn traverse. The cost is that it is fully exposed at the high point of the Pacific Crest Trail in Washington, with no water, no wind shelter and no retreat that is not a long descent. The history is the warning: weather arrives here fast and out of season.

sites.name: Chambers Lake Campground
sites.capacity: A small forested campground with basic single and double sites; first come, first served
sites.water: No potable water on site — bring your own or filter from the lake. Vault toilets are provided
sites.permit: No wilderness permit needed for the campground itself, since it sits outside the boundary. A modest per-night fee has been charged in some seasons and waived in others, so carry cash and check the board on arrival. A Northwest Forest Pass is still required at Berry Patch and the Snowgrass trailhead a short distance up the road.
sites.notes: The obvious drive-in base for the Goat Rocks crest, under a mile from both the Berry Patch and Snowgrass trailheads, so you can sleep at the car and be walking at first light without the four-mile carry to Snowgrass. That makes it the right choice for a car-to-car attempt on Old Snowy, and a sensible staging night before shouldering a pack for Ives or Gilbert. It is heavily timbered and low, so there is no view and no acclimatisation value, and the approach roads are long gravel with washboard — allow more driving time than the mileage suggests. Snow closes the access road well into spring, which is the practical limit on early-season attempts from this side.

sites.name: Conrad Meadows and Surprise Lake, South Fork Tieton
sites.capacity: Primitive dispersed and stock camping in the broad meadows at the road end, and established backcountry sites at Surprise Lake several miles up the loop; no reservations and no numbered sites
sites.water: The South Fork Tieton and its tributaries throughout, and the lake itself higher up; abundant by the standards of the range's east side but still to be treated
sites.permit: Free self-issued wilderness permit at the trailhead board once you cross into the wilderness. Camping is prohibited within 100 feet of lakes. Note this trailhead sits on the drier eastern forest rather than the Gifford Pinchot side, so confirm which parking pass the board is asking for before leaving the car. Heavy stock use means the meadows are shared with horse parties.
sites.notes: This is the correct side of the range for Gilbert Peak's Conrad Glacier and Meade Glacier routes, and there is no sensible way to reach either from the Snowgrass trailheads — the two approaches are separated by the whole crest. From the road end the trail runs level through meadows for around four miles before the loop divides, and the northern fork leads toward Surprise Lake and eventually the benches, waterfall and Barren Lake below the Conrad Glacier. Most parties camp once in the basin and climb from there, since the glacier and the traverse across the Meade to Gilbert's south ridge make for a long day on their own. The meadows at the road end are a legitimate first night if you arrive late, but they are low, buggy in early summer and a long way from anything. This side is far quieter than Snowgrass, and the corresponding cost is a much longer approach and much less traffic if something goes wrong.

sites.name: Climbers Bivouac
sites.capacity: Around fourteen small primitive tent sites, close together, first come and first served only; motorhomes and trailers are directed elsewhere
sites.water: None. There is no water at the trailhead, so carry everything you need for the night and for the climb. Pit toilets are provided
sites.permit: Camping itself is free, but the parking requires a Northwest Forest Pass, an Interagency pass, or a small day fee. SEPARATELY AND UNAVOIDABLY, a climbing permit is required year round for anyone going above 4,800 feet on the mountain, and camping above 4,800 feet is prohibited outright. From April 1 to October 31 that permit carries a daily quota and a per-climber fee of about twenty dollars: 350 climbers a day from April 1 to May 14, then only 110 a day from May 15 through October 31. Permits are sold first come, first served with no lottery, released a month at a time on the first day of the preceding month at seven in the morning Pacific time, and the summer dates sell out within minutes of release. From November 1 to March 31 the permit is free and self-issued at the trailhead with no quota. Blue bags are mandatory for all human waste above the tree line and are stocked at the trailhead kiosk.
sites.notes: The summer roadhead for Monitor Ridge, and effectively the only place to sleep close to that route, since the mountain above 4,800 feet is closed to camping. It is a rough clearing in second-growth timber at the end of a Forest Service road, with tent pads and fire rings but nothing else, and the sites are small and packed in. The value is purely positional: the summit trail leaves from here and a night at the trailhead turns a long day into a manageable one. Plan the permit before the campsite, because the permit is the real constraint — the quota tightens sharply in mid-May, and the whole summer sells on release day. Arrive with your blue bag and use it; there is a composting toilet where the trail meets the tree line, and above that there is nothing at all.

sites.name: Marble Mountain Sno-Park
sites.capacity: Two large plowed lots plus adjacent forest; winter parties routinely pitch tents in and beside the lots, so capacity is generous and informal rather than defined
sites.water: None liquid in winter — melt snow, and carry water in the shoulder seasons. Two vault toilets are provided, and a warming hut is open through the winter months
sites.permit: A Washington Sno-Park permit is required from December 1 to March 31, and this is a non-motorised area. The Mount St. Helens climbing permit is still required for anyone above 4,800 feet, but through the winter window it is free, self-issued at the trailhead and unlimited — the single easiest time of year to climb this mountain from a paperwork point of view. The 4,800-foot camping prohibition applies in winter exactly as it does in summer.
sites.notes: The winter and shoulder-season staging point, and the start of the Worm Flows route when the road to Climbers Bivouac is under snow. It is lower than the summer trailhead, so Worm Flows carries a bigger day at roughly 5,700 feet of gain, which is the main argument for sleeping here rather than driving in the dark. Camping in a plowed parking lot is not scenic and it works: the lots are large, the toilets are open and the warming hut takes the edge off a cold morning. Parties commonly move up to camp on the snow around the Chocolate Falls area on the way, which stays below the 4,800-foot line if you site it carefully — check your altimeter rather than guessing, because that boundary is a legal one. Avalanche conditions on the Worm Flows gullies, not the permit, are the season's real gate.
